title: Law & Your Rights · Episode 3
chapters: The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born
Making a complaint that actually gets results

units.t: Law & Your Rights. Episode three.
In this episode: The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born, Your rights as a consumer and Making a complaint that actually gets results.
Part one. The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born.
A woman in a Scottish café sipped a ginger beer and claimed she found a rotting snail in it.
Her lawsuit changed the law for almost everyone in the English-speaking world.
A snail and no contract.
On 26 August 1928, May Donoghue drank ginger beer from a dark, opaque bottle at the Wellmeadow Café in Paisley, near Glasgow.
A friend had bought it.
When the rest was poured into her ice cream float, she later said, the decomposed remains of a snail slid into her glass.
She claimed shock and gastroenteritis.
The trouble was legal.
If a faulty product hurt you, your main route was usually to sue the seller for breach of contract.
She had no contract with the café owner, who had neither made the drink nor sealed the bottle.
She had none with the manufacturer, David Stevenson, either.
Earlier cases suggested that a manufacturer owed nothing to a stranger, except for inherently dangerous items.
Up to the Lords.
Mrs Donoghue had little money, so she was allowed to sue as a pauper, without paying the usual court costs.
Her lawyer, Walter Leechman, took on the manufacturer.
The case reached the House of Lords, then Britain's highest court, which ruled in May 1932.
The judges did not decide whether a snail had really been in the bottle.
They answered a preliminary question: assuming everything she said was true, did the law give her a claim?
By three votes to two, they said yes.
A manufacturer who sells a product meant to reach the consumer unchanged owes that consumer a duty to take reasonable care.
Who is my neighbour.
The most famous judgment came from Lord Atkin, who reached for the parable of the Good Samaritan, in which a lawyer asks, 'Who is my neighbour?'
Atkin gave a legal answer.
You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour.
And your neighbour is anyone so closely and directly affected by what you do that you ought to have them in mind.
This was a broad principle, not a narrow rule about ginger beer.
A duty of care can exist between strangers wherever harm is foreseeable and the relationship is close enough.
Lawyers call it the neighbour principle, and first-year law students still learn it.
What negligence requires.
Donoghue v Stevenson gave shape to negligence, the law of careless harm.
Broadly, a person suing must show three things.
First, the other side owed them a duty of care.
Second, the other side breached it by falling below the standard of a reasonable person in their position.
Third, the breach actually caused harm of a kind the law recognises.
These ideas now sit behind claims about car crashes, medical mistakes, slippery supermarket floors and unsafe buildings.
Courts have spent decades refining where duties begin and end, because a duty that stretched forever would make everyone liable for everything.
Many places, including Australian states, have also passed laws limiting some claims and damages.
The snail travels.
A Scottish decision about a Paisley café could have stayed local.
Instead, in the mid-1930s, an Australian case reached the Privy Council in London, then Australia's final court of appeal.
Doctor Richard Grant had developed severe dermatitis from woollen underwear made by Australian Knitting Mills, which contained irritating chemicals left from manufacturing.
Relying on Donoghue v Stevenson, the Privy Council held the manufacturer liable.
Courts in Canada and New Zealand followed, and governments later built consumer protection laws on these foundations.
Here is the twist.
David Stevenson died before the trial on the facts, and the claim was settled out of court.
No judge ever ruled on whether the snail existed.
A memorial now marks the café site.
The key idea: A woman who said she found a snail in her ginger beer had no contract with anyone, so the old law seemed to leave her without a remedy.
Part two. Your rights as a consumer.
'No refunds' signs, 'take it up with the manufacturer', 'the warranty's expired'.
Australian consumer law says otherwise more often than you think.
One national law.
Since 1 January 2011, one national law, the Australian Consumer Law, has protected consumers across Australia.
It sits in a schedule to the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and applies the same way in every state and territory.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, ACCC, enforces it, together with agencies such as NSW Fair Trading and Consumer Affairs Victoria.
It covers consumer guarantees, product safety, misleading conduct, unfair contract terms, unsolicited selling and more.
You are generally a consumer if you buy goods or services normally used for personal or household purposes, or anything costing up to $100,000.
Guarantees and remedies.
Consumer guarantees apply automatically, whatever the receipt or store policy says, and businesses can't exclude them.
Goods must be of acceptable quality, safe, durable, free from defects, for a reasonable time, fit for any purpose you told the seller about, and match their description.
Services need due care and skill and must be delivered in reasonable time.
A $2,000 fridge should last far longer than a $20 kettle.
For a major failure, such as an unsafe item or one you wouldn't have bought knowing the problem, you can choose a refund or replacement, or keep it and claim compensation.
For a minor failure, the business can choose to repair, replace or refund.
If it refuses or takes too long, you can get it fixed elsewhere and claim reasonable costs.
Refund myths.
You have no legal right to a refund just because you changed your mind; that's store policy.
But 'no refunds' signs are misleading if they suggest you have no rights when goods are faulty.
The retailer can't send you to the manufacturer.
Proof of purchase can be a bank statement or online order, not only the receipt.
Sale items are covered too, unless the defect was pointed out before you bought.
A manufacturer's warranty is a promise on top of your guarantees, not a replacement.
Guarantees can continue after the warranty ends if a product fails sooner than expected.
Before buying an extended warranty, ask what it offers beyond the law.
Misleading conduct and scams.
The law bans misleading or deceptive conduct in trade.
That includes false claims about quality or origin, fake 'was' prices that inflate a discount, and fine print that contradicts the headline offer.
Businesses must generally show a single total price including compulsory fees, not hide charges until the end, drip pricing.
Large supermarkets must show unit prices, such as price per 100 grams.
Exploiting someone who clearly doesn't understand a deal, unconscionable conduct, is also prohibited.
Scams include fake parcel texts, calls impersonating banks or police, investment schemes and romance scams.
Warning signs are pressure to act now, unusual payments like gift cards or crypto, and requests for personal details or remote access.
Call back on a number you find yourself.
If you've lost money, contact your bank, then report to Scamwatch.
IDCARE offers free support.
Door-to-door and phone sales.
If a seller knocks on your door or phones you out of the blue and you agree to buy something worth more than $100, the law treats it as an unsolicited consumer agreement.
You get a cooling-off period of 10 business days to change your mind, and the seller can't take any payment during that time.
Door-to-door sellers can generally visit only between 9am and 6pm on weekdays and until 5pm on Saturdays, and not on Sundays or public holidays, unless you've made an appointment.
They must tell you that you can ask them to leave, and go straight away when you do.
If a business won't honour your rights, your state or territory fair trading agency can help.
This lesson is general information only.
The key idea: The Australian Consumer Law gives the same protections in every state and territory, enforced by the ACCC and state agencies.
Part three. Making a complaint that actually gets results.
Knowing your rights is one thing; getting a business to honour them is another.
Here is the step by step path from polite email to independent ombudsman.
Goal and evidence.
Consider a washing machine that dies a fortnight after its warranty ends.
Angry calls get nowhere; clarity works.
Write down what went wrong, when, and what you want: a repair, replacement, refund or compensation.
Then check Australian Consumer Law.
Its consumer guarantees mean goods must be of acceptable quality and last a reasonable time, regardless of any manufacturer's warranty, and a major failure gives you a choice of remedy.
The ACCC, accc.
gov.
au, explains this in plain English.
Gather proof of purchase, photos or video of the fault, and any packaging.
Start a log of every call, email and visit, with the date, the person and what they said or promised, including any sales claims.
It makes your complaint precise, and shows you tried to resolve things first.
This is general information, not legal advice.
Complain in writing.
Most problems are fixed at the first step, so give the business a genuine chance.
Ask to speak with someone who can make decisions, often a manager or the complaints team rather than front counter staff.
Be polite, specific and firm.
If that does not work, put your complaint in writing by email or letter.
Briefly set out what you bought, the problem, what you have done so far and the remedy you want.
Refer to the consumer guarantees if relevant, and give a reasonable deadline, such as 14 days, for a response.
Many large businesses must have an internal dispute resolution process, and asking for your complaint to be formally logged often moves it to more senior people.
Fair trading and ombudsmen.
For most goods and services, contact your state fair trading agency, such as NSW Fair Trading or Consumer Affairs Victoria.
They can advise and may contact the business for you.
The ACCC enforces the law nationally but generally does not resolve individual disputes.

Several industries have free, independent ombudsman schemes: the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman for phone and internet, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority for banks, insurers and super funds, and state energy and water ombudsmen.
Most require you to complain to the business first.
The scheme sends your complaint back to senior staff for a last chance to fix it, and many settle there.
If not, it investigates and may recommend or decide an outcome.
With AFCA, a decision you accept can bind the business, and you can still go to court if you reject it.
Tribunals and chargebacks.
If no ombudsman covers the business and the fair trading agency cannot resolve it, a state tribunal or local court can hear consumer claims.
Examples include NCAT in New South Wales, VCAT in Victoria and QCAT in Queensland.
Small claims processes are designed to be cheaper and less formal than ordinary courts, though there is usually a filing fee and you present your own case with your evidence.
Separately, if you paid by credit or debit card and the goods never arrived or the business has collapsed, ask your bank about a chargeback.
Card schemes have rules for disputed transactions, and banks set time limits for requests, so contact them as soon as you realise there is a problem.
Tone and persistence.
The most effective complainers are rarely the loudest.
Staff who are shouted at tend to follow the script; staff who are treated respectfully often look for a way to help.
Keep messages short and factual, repeat your requested remedy clearly, and do not accept vague promises without a date.
If you are offered less than you asked for, consider whether it is fair rather than rejecting it on principle, since time and stress have costs too.
Public reviews and social media posts can attract attention, but stick to accurate facts to avoid defamation risks.
Finally, report scams and misleading conduct to the ACCC or Scamwatch, even if you get your money back.
It helps protect the next customer.
The key idea: Decide the outcome you want, know your consumer guarantees, and keep evidence and a log.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did Mrs Donoghue seem to have no legal claim?
Answer. She had no contract with the seller or the maker of the drink.
Question two. Who enforces the Australian Consumer Law?
Answer. The ACCC and state fair trading agencies.
Question three. What do consumer guarantees mean for a product that fails soon after its warranty ends?
Answer. Goods must be of acceptable quality and last a reasonable time.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
